lesson.title: When the Guarantee Breaks: Why Continuity and a Closed Interval Both Matter
lesson.summary: Both hypotheses of the Extreme Value Theorem, continuity of the function and a closed, bounded interval, are genuinely necessary; remove either one and the guarantee of a maximum or minimum can fail.
lesson.body:
The Extreme Value Theorem is a conditional statement: continuity plus a closed interval implies existence of a max and a min. It is tempting to assume the conditions are just technical fine print, but each one is load bearing. Drop either condition and it is possible to build a function that has no global maximum, no global minimum, or neither, even though the function looks perfectly reasonable.

Start with the closed, bounded interval requirement. Consider f(x) = 1/x on the interval (0, 1]. This interval is half open, it is missing its left endpoint at 0, so it is not closed. The function itself is continuous everywhere on its domain, there is no break in the graph anywhere on (0, 1]. But watch what happens as x approaches 0 from the right, inside the domain: f(x) = 1/x grows without bound, racing off toward infinity. There is no largest value, no matter how far out you look there is always a larger one just past it, so no global maximum exists. Interestingly, a global minimum does exist here: since f is decreasing on (0, 1], its smallest value occurs at the right endpoint, f(1) = 1. This shows that violating one condition does not necessarily destroy both extreme values, it simply removes the theorem's guarantee that they must exist; here it happened to spare the minimum but not the maximum.

Now consider the continuity requirement, holding the interval fixed and closed. Define f piecewise on the closed, bounded interval [0, 1]: let f(x) = x for every x with 0 <= x < 1, and separately define f(1) = 0. The domain is exactly [0, 1], which is closed and bounded, satisfying that half of the theorem. But f has a jump discontinuity at x = 1, since the values of f(x) climb steadily toward 1 as x approaches 1 from the left, yet f actually equals 0 right at x = 1. Ask whether f attains a maximum value. For every x in [0, 1), f(x) = x is strictly less than 1. And f(1) = 0, which is also less than 1. So no input in the domain ever produces the output 1, even though 1 is exactly the value the function keeps approaching. The supremum of 1 is approached but never reached, so there is no global maximum, despite a perfectly closed and bounded domain.

Both counterexamples fail for a related reason: something escapes. In the first, values escape to infinity because the domain has a hole letting inputs sneak arbitrarily close to a boundary that was never included. In the second, values escape a gap because the function jumps away from the value it was approaching right at the critical input. Continuity closes that second kind of gap, and a closed, bounded interval closes the first kind. Together, the two conditions leave no way for a supremum or infimum to be merely approached rather than actually attained, which is exactly why the Extreme Value Theorem can promise attainment rather than just a limiting value.
